ExecConfigSweep.description:
Execution config with base values and optional sweep axes.

Each axis dict: ``{"param", "min", "max", "n", "mode"?}``. ``n`` is a
RUN-COUNT MULTIPLIER in every mode — a swept axis contributes n values
and the plan crosses all axes (∏n variants per base run). ``mode``
("grid" | "random", optional) selects how the n values are generated,
independently of the experiment's signal ``search_mode``:

- ``grid``: the n evenly-spaced linspace(min, max, n) points.
- ``random``: n fresh independent Uniform(min, max) draws.

When ``mode`` is absent the plan path's default applies (grid plans →
"grid", random plans → "random").
ExecConfigSweep.title: ExecConfigSweep

ExperimentConfig.description:
Full experiment configuration -- the top-level object.

- random: randomly sample N runs (signals, params, exec config all random)

A pair of OHLCV files for a continuous-allocation rotation experiment.

synthetic A/B ratio frame for kb signal evaluation.
PairSelection.title: PairSelection

ParamSweep.description:
One sampling axis: how many values to take from a range, and how.

Either explicit ``values``, or a ``[min, max]`` range with ``n`` samples
drawn in ``mode`` -- ``grid`` takes the n evenly-spaced points, ``random``
takes n independent draws. ``n`` is the count in both; the mode only
decides which values, never how many. Unset ``n`` and ``mode`` take the
experiment's ``param_samples`` and ``search_mode``.

``step`` is the same axis written as an interval, kept so saved configs
still load. It is read once and translated to ``n``; nothing writes it.
ParamSweep.title: ParamSweep

PinnedStrategy.description:
One strategy, run unchanged on every window of a condition study.

A study varies the market and nothing else, so this is the whole strategy
and there is no sampling axis anywhere near it: the same ``entry``,
``exit`` and ``exec_config`` reach every run verbatim. That is what makes
a study's answer about the market rather than about a search.

``source_strategy_id`` is the caller's own identifier for the strategy
(MangroveAI's strategy UUID). Stamped on every row so a study's results can
be joined back to the strategy they describe, and so a second study of the
same strategy is recognisable as one.

SignalGroup.description:
A named pool of signals for within-group random sampling.

Each strategy sampled from a group draws ALL of its signals — entry AND
exit, triggers AND filters — only from this group's members, so signals
from different groups never co-occur on one strategy (e.g. keep volatility
and momentum apart by putting them in separate groups).

Membership = every non-blacklisted signal whose category is in
``categories``, PLUS ``include`` (specific signal names forced in even if
their category isn't listed), MINUS ``exclude`` (specific signal names
removed). ``weight`` is the group's relative share of the total strategy
count; ``None`` on a group means "even split with the other unweighted
groups". Weights are normalized across all groups.

``triggers`` and ``filters`` divide that membership by role. A role
selection is applied to the group's members, never in place of them, so it
can only name signals the group already holds; one that names nothing, or
is absent, gives that role every member. A signal is eligible only for the
role its knowledge-base type gives it, so a role selection chooses which of
the group's members serve that role rather than reassigning them.
SignalGroup.title: SignalGroup

SignalGroupRole.description:
One role's share of a signal group, by the group's own membership rule.

Same ``(categories union include) minus exclude`` formula a group uses,
applied to the trigger or the filter pools alone.
SignalGroupRole.title: SignalGroupRole

carries no ``param_samples`` and reads empty as the whole pool.

get.description:
List the windows a sweep can select, with regime labels where we have them.

A window is listed only when its market's series covers it and its warm-up
(``series_coverage.runnable``); the verdict comes from the series index,
never from a series. Labels are attached here rather than inside ``discover_datasets`` because the
regime labeller itself enumerates the catalog — having discovery read the table
it is about to write would be circular.

Cached, because the dataset picker calls this on mount and discovery reads every
CSV in the corpus to count bars (5.5s for 4,103 files). Off the event loop for the
same reason: a 5s synchronous walk in an async handler blocks every other request
on the worker, and this endpoint is not the only thing the Configure view loads.

The cache is keyed on the catalog generation as well as the clock. Every cache
here is a module global, so a create invalidates only the process that served
it, and a deployment runs more than one. The manifest is rewritten by every
create, so its generation reports whether any instance has changed the catalog,
at the cost of one metadata call per listing.

A range longer than MAX_BARS bars is shortened to the whole days that fit,

- deployed-error: an evaluation error occurred
- deployed-heartbeat: periodic liveness pulse

get.description:
List experiments the caller may see — summary view, no live progress.

Returns only the persisted config fields. Live progress (parquet
flush count, reconciled "running" → "completed" transitions) is
expensive: each experiment requires a separate GCS LIST call. The
prior implementation did this in an N+1 loop and pushed past the
gateway 60s timeout once the experiment catalog grew past ~50
entries (observed on prod 2026-05-31: 504 upstream timeout).

Callers needing live progress should hit
``GET /experiments/{experiment_id}`` per experiment of interest
— that endpoint does the GCS read once for the single row the
caller is actually inspecting.

The ``status`` field here reflects the last-persisted state on
the config row. For a "running" experiment it may lag the actual
GCS parquet-count state until the next progress poll reconciles
it. ``completed`` is populated from ONE grouped native-table query
(finalized sweeps only — the native table fills at finalize); for
in-flight or unmerged experiments it stays None so callers don't
treat the list view as a live-progress source.

Sync on purpose: FastAPI runs a sync handler in its threadpool, so the
blocking store read below never holds the event loop (#588).

get.description:
The per-sweep caps THIS caller will actually be judged against.

Read straight off ``request.state`` — the very values
``validate_experiment`` gates on, injected by the upstream proxy from the
caller's tier. A client that displays these cannot show a limit the gate
does not apply.

It exists because the builder carried its own copy of the tier table, with
a hardcoded number per tier. When the caller's forwarded tier and the
client's idea of it disagreed, the wizard sized a sweep to 5,000 runs that
the gate then refused at 1,000 — and the wizard had no candle number at
all, so the candle cap could only ever be discovered by being rejected.

``0`` means no cap is enforced for this caller (internal callers, and any
proxy that injects no cap headers). ``-1`` means unlimited.

get.description:
First-class query surface for persisted per-run trades (#370).

Sync on purpose: the trades read can download many chunk files, and an
``async`` handler doing that blocking read held the event loop, so every
other request to the instance (a 50ms ``/strategy``) waited it out. FastAPI
runs a sync handler in its threadpool (same reasoning as #588).

Reads the trades parquet persisted at sweep time (#359) from
``cloud/trades/org_id=<X>/<exp>/**`` (keyed by ``run_index``) instead of
re-running the backtest — unlike ``visualize``, which embeds trades in a
chart response. Tenant access is enforced by the router-level
``require_experiment_access`` dependency; the org partition is the owning
org of the experiment, which the sweep stamps on every trade. Rows are
returned in stable ``entry_timestamp`` order,
paginated by ``limit``/``offset``.

An optional timezone-aware ``as_of`` freezes pagination to the same
snapshot as result curves. Only known entry timestamps after the cutoff
are excluded; rows with absent or malformed timestamps remain inspectable.

``persisted=false`` means the experiment predates trade persistence (no
artifact); callers wanting trades for those should use the visualize
endpoint, which re-runs to regenerate them.

Trade rows are keyed by ``run_index`` alone, and an index can name several
runs (MangroveOracle#782). Such an index answers 409 ``ambiguous_run`` unless
``config_hash``/``data_file_path`` names one; a named run's trades are read
by the config_hash stamped on each trade row, or -- trades written before
the stamp -- from its own dataset_key, and when another run at the index
shares that dataset_key the trades cannot be split and the answer is 409
``run_trades_not_separable`` -- never the two runs' trades merged.

post.description: Run candidate strategies through the Mangrove SIEVE go/no-go gate and return predicted probabilities. Accepts either a list of MangroveAI-shaped Strategy objects (`strategies`) or a list of raw run dicts (`runs`) — exactly one must be provided. Each response item carries the binary go/no-go head (`p_no_trades`, `p_trades`) — whether a strategy is worth backtesting (will it place trades). SIEVE does NOT predict performance; the retired 4-class outcome head is no longer returned. Responses are provenance-stamped with `model_version` (a content hash of the bundled artifacts) and `code_version` (Oracle + MangroveAI + KB + Roots refs). Per-request cap: 99 items.

400.description: Both or neither of `strategies` / `runs` provided, or empty

List available signals from the knowledge base.

    type: Filter by signal type (TRIGGER or FILTER).
    search: Substring filter on signal name.
    catalog: Keep only signals a selection catalogue names -- repeat it to
        allow several, and a signal any one of them names is kept. Known
        catalogues are ``indicators`` and ``candlestick_patterns``.

get.description:
The selection catalogues, resolved against the signals we have.

Each entry carries the signals of it that are actually in the pool, so a
chip built from this counts what selecting it would reach, and ``missing``
names anything the catalogue lists that the knowledge base no longer
offers. ``sources`` is where the entry list was drawn from, so a selection
made with it can be traced back to what it was based on.
